text: Lessons 9 through 11 built the full picture of an incident: every related alert pulled together, a reconstructed timeline, and a confirmed scope of everything the attacker touched. Severity classification decides how serious that incident actually is - and it isn't just about how technically clever the attack was or how many systems got touched.

In practice, severity depends on four factors. Business impact asks what's actually disrupted - a single workstation offline is very different from order processing going down. Data sensitivity asks what kind of data was involved - internal notes versus customer payment card data carry very different weight. Scope and spread is the direct payoff of Lesson 11's scoping work. Regulatory implications asks whether the data involved triggers a legal notification requirement, like HIPAA or PCI DSS.

Compare two incidents with nearly identical technical details, both starting with phishing and ending in lateral movement. One hits a junior employee's account with access to nothing but internal documents, and scoping confirms no further spread - a moderate incident. The other hits an account with access to a payment card database, scoping confirms the attacker queried it, and PCI DSS notification now applies - the same attack chain, but a critical incident.

Severity isn't a filing label - it decides how many people get pulled in and how fast. A low-severity incident might stay with the on-call analyst. A high-severity incident pulls in the IR team lead and starts executive briefings. A critical incident with regulatory exposure can mean legal counsel and board notification within hours.

Setting severity too low means the wrong-sized team responds to a problem that actually needed far more people and far faster escalation. That's why severity classification has to be accurate, not just fast, and why it's revisited as new scoping information comes in. Next, Chapter 4 opens with containment strategies, starting with the real tradeoffs between short-term and long-term containment.
